co_citadel_the_3.blurb: A big domed buttress on Lumpy Ridge above Estes Park, sitting high above its neighbour The Pear. Twelve climbs are on record, mostly traditional multipitch with a couple of aid lines, spread from easy terrain through a cluster of 5.10 leads, with one or two far harder pitches at the top end. A large right-facing dihedral near the middle of the face defines the cliff, and its best-known line follows that corner. The base is guarded by low-angle slabs and some fourth-class scrambling, and the stone is mostly good with a few decomposed patches. It sees few visitors, which suits climbers who want quiet and are comfortable with a committing approach.

co_waterfall_boulder.blurb: One boulder in the Wolf Creek Pass bouldering zone near South Fork, in the high country where late summer is the cool-season pick. A dozen problems are recorded here, running from an easy warm-up through a solid middle band of V4 to V5, a trio around V7, and a few much harder lines reaching double-digit V grades. Quality varies: several problems are rated well while a couple are weak, so it works best as one stop in a larger day among the neighbouring boulders along the highway rather than a destination by itself.

co_sail_the.blurb: A freestanding formation in the Triple Tier area of Poudre Canyon, west of Fort Collins, and visible from the road not long after The Mish. The twelve climbs here are mostly bolted sport lines with a couple of trad leads, and the grades lean hard: one route around 5.8 and one around 5.10, then a big block of 5.11s, several 5.12s, and a single 5.13 at the top. It is a good spot for climbers already comfortable on steeper face and want a concentrated set of difficult pitches rather than moderates. Reaching it takes a short hike beyond the neighbouring Upper Echelon wall.

co_thindependence.blurb: A steep granite wall on Independence Pass, east of Aspen at roughly 9,800 feet, just past the Grotto Wall complex and close to Outrageous Overhangs. Dense trees hide it until you are underneath, then every route is in view. Of the twelve climbs, most are bolted sport with a pair of trad lines, and nothing is below 5.10: expect two at 5.10, a big group at 5.11, and a few 5.12s. The face looks south and west, so it can feel warm on summer afternoons. It rewards climbers who want steep, sustained pitches in a short walk from the highway.

co_waterfall_wall.blurb: A quartzite wall in the gorge south of Ouray, set beside a waterfall on the far side of the canyon from the highway. Twelve routes mix trad and bolted sport, mostly from 5.7 up through the 5.10s, with a few harder at 5.11 and 5.12. The stone has plenty of sidepulls and rewards balance and careful footwork. Getting in is a real commitment: you cross or rappel into the canyon and then climb out, with no easy bail, so it suits experienced parties with a long rope who watch the weather, since storms can build quickly in this setting.

co_roog_s_wall.blurb: A long, low bouldering wall in the Morrison, Evergreen and Littleton cluster, at about 6,100 feet and a short walk across the footbridge near the Green Mountain trailhead. Twelve problems are recorded, mostly easy: four at the V0 grade or below, a handful at V1 and V2, and a few V4 and V5 problems for those wanting more. The east end is sturdier and offers good grip work for beginners, while the west end is more delicate and more likely to break, so tread lightly there. It can get very hot by mid-morning, and mountain bikers share the trail.

co_skinner_mountain.blurb: A small wall in the Buffalo Creek zone of the South Platte, found along CO 126 south of Pine, and one of the easier crags there to locate. Twelve climbs combine cracks and moderate bolted slabs, mostly two- or three-pitch lines with straightforward walk-offs. Grades are gentle: a few at 5.5 to 5.6, a bunch in the 5.7 to 5.9 range, a couple of 5.10s and a single 5.11. That makes it a sensible place to build multipitch experience, and an easy trad lead is among the favourites. The walk in is roughly fifteen minutes on a faint, cairned trail heading west.

co_renaissance_wall.blurb: A tall granite wall tucked into a slot-like cleft within the Book formation on Lumpy Ridge. Unlike the low-angle slabs the ridge is known for, this one is steep and technical, demanding precise footwork and crimping. Of its twelve climbs, ten are trad and two are sport, with a couple at 5.9, three 5.10s, three 5.11s, and a strong group of 5.12 and 5.13 testpieces. Rock improves higher up but loose, chossy sections turn up throughout, so watch for rockfall. The enclosed setting brings welcome relief from hot summer sun, making it a good option on warm days for strong climbers.
